title: How your phone guesses your word
interaction: Type a word with a slip in it and watch the phone's two counts: which real words are one or two changes away, and how often each of those is used in a huge pile of books. The suggestion is the common one that is close; type a rare name and watch it 'corrected' into a common word. Then type the start of a sentence and see the next-word guesses, which are nothing but a count of which word most often followed the last one in the pile; change the last word and the counts change.
takeaway: A phone guesses your word by counting: which real words are nearest to what you typed and which are used most, so it is confidently wrong whenever you are unusual.
needs: Word and word-pair counts: a subset of the Google Books Ngram data (1-grams and 2-grams, CC BY 3.0, https://storage.googleapis.com/books/ngrams/books/datasetsv3.html), or counts the page builds itself from a Project Gutenberg text (public domain).
needsSource: Google Books Ngram (CC BY 3.0) and/or a public-domain book; Norvig's count_1w and count_2w files derive from the Google Web Trillion Word corpus with no stated data terms, so not those.
pitfall: The phone does not understand the sentence and is not reading your mind; it also learns your own words by counting them. Do not call the next-word counts a language model with a network: here it is a table of counts, and language-models is where the network comes in.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 4, Natural Interaction, in the AAAI/CSTA K-12 AI guidelines (https://ai4k12.org/); the nearest existing page is level 2.
overlapWith: language-models (level 2): that page shows a real network's next-token probabilities and sampling; this one has no network, only edit distance and counted word pairs, and the suggestions can be checked by hand.

title: Why a photo cannot unlock your phone
interaction: Turn a head in front of a drawn phone: the phone sprays a pattern of thousands of invisible dots onto it, a second camera sees where each dot lands, and the page shows the depth map they measure, nose nearest, ears farthest. Enrol the head, then present it again turned, smiling or with glasses: the map differs a little and the match bar stays above the line. Hold up a flat photo of the same face and every dot lands at the same depth, so the bar collapses; present a twin's head with the same shape and the bar stays up.
takeaway: Face unlock measures the shape of your face in depth from where a pattern of dots lands, so a flat photo fails while a face with the same shape, a twin, can pass.
needs: A head to measure: a simple parametric head drawn on the page (no external data), or a scanned head if one under an open licence is confirmed.
needsSource: none; depth is computed by triangulating projected dots against the head's surface on the page.
pitfall: It is not reading your eyes or your DNA, and a match is a score above a line, never certainty; the phone follows gradual changes such as a beard by updating the stored map. Name the depth method as one kind (structured light) and say that other phones use other depth tricks.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 1, Perception (https://ai4k12.org/); 'Face ID' averaged about 14,500 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Face_ID/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: fingerprint-match in this batch: the same enough-points-agree rule on ridges; light-optics (level 1) has the ray model. medical-imaging reconstructs a slice from many shadows; here depth comes from where projected dots land.

title: How a phone knows your finger
interaction: Press a finger on a drawn sensor and see what it sees: a small patch of ridges, not the whole print, with the ridge ends and forks marked as dots, which are all the phone keeps. Press again, sliding and turning the finger or pressing only a corner, and watch the match count, how many dots line up, rise or fall past the 'enough' line. Wet the finger or put a cut across it and lose a few dots; press a different finger and watch almost none line up.
takeaway: A phone stores a map of where your ridges end and fork, not a picture, and unlocks when enough of those points line up, never all of them.
needs: Fingerprint images generated on the page with a published synthetic-fingerprint model (an orientation field with cores and deltas filtered into ridges, as in SFinGe, Cappelli et al. 2000), stated on the page as synthetic; the FVC benchmark databases are research-use only and are not shipped.
needsSource: none shipped; synthetic ridges from a published model, with the minutiae extracted by thinning. Real fingerprint databases (FVC, NIST SD) are not openly licensed.
pitfall: The match is never total: a threshold decides, so a dirty or cut finger can fail and, rarely, a stranger can pass. The phone keeps no image of the print, and the sensor reads a patch, which is why enrolment asks for many presses.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 1, Perception (https://ai4k12.org/); 'Fingerprint' averaged about 17,700 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Fingerprint/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: face-unlock-depth in this batch: the same decision rule, enough points agree, on a different measurement; cryptography (level 2) is how the secret is kept. Nothing existing shows a biometric match.

title: How a spam filter decides
interaction: A pile of real text messages arrives, each already marked spam or not; pick any word, 'free', 'win', 'tonight', 'mum', and see two counts, how many spam messages contain it and how many ordinary ones. Build the filter by letting it count every word, then write a message of your own and watch the words vote: each nudges the score toward spam or not according to its two counts. Try to sneak past with 'fr33' and watch the vote change; mark your message and see the counts update.
takeaway: A spam filter has no idea what a message means: it counts which words turned up more in past spam, which is why spammers misspell and why your 'report spam' clicks teach it.
needs: The SMS Spam Collection (Almeida and Hidalgo, UCI Machine Learning Repository, 5,574 messages, CC BY 4.0), or a subset.
needsSource: UCI SMS Spam Collection, CC BY 4.0 (https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/228/sms+spam+collection).
pitfall: No word is bad: 'free' is only commoner in spam. The filter can be fooled both ways, and how much spam exists overall matters, so a rare kind of message needs stronger evidence; keep that as counts, not Bayes' formula.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 3, Learning, in the AAAI/CSTA K-12 AI guidelines (https://ai4k12.org/).
overlapWith: bayes-theorem (level 1) counts true and false positives in a grid of 1,000 people and learning-from-data fits a curve; this page builds the simplest real classifier on a real corpus, with word counts the reader can check.

title: How a phone counts your steps
interaction: Play a real recording from a phone on someone's waist as they walk, climb stairs, sit and stand, with the stretches labelled: a line jiggles with every stride. Set the 'that was a step' line and watch the counter: too low and the fidgets during the sitting stretches count as steps, too high and the gentle strolling stretches are missed. Then shake the phone in a drawn car on a bumpy road and watch the counter climb without anyone walking.
takeaway: A step counter counts jolts of a shaking sensor, so it needs a line between a stride and a fidget, and a bumpy ride can count as a walk.
needs: Continuous raw accelerometer traces at 50 samples a second, with activity labels, from the Smartphone-Based Recognition of Human Activities and Postural Transitions dataset (UCI, CC BY 4.0).
needsSource: UCI HAPT dataset, CC BY 4.0 (https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/341/smartphone+based+recognition+of+human+activities+and+postural+transitions). It labels activity stretches but records no step counts, so there is no step ground truth: false counts are steps counted while sitting or standing, and the walking count is judged against the strides visible in the trace. The bumpy-car trace is synthesised and said to be.
pitfall: The phone does not sense feet or use GPS to count steps; it counts jolts. Show the misses and the false counts, not a perfect counter.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 1, Perception: 'computers perceive the world using sensors' (https://ai4k12.org/); 'Pedometer' averaged about 3,800 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025.
overlapWith: newtons-laws (level 1) is forces and motion and feedback-control reads sensors into a controller; nothing existing counts events in a real sensor trace.

title: Teach a machine to tell things apart
interaction: Draw a few cats and a few houses (or pull examples from a pile of other people's doodles), label them, and draw a new one: the machine shrinks every drawing to a small grid of squares, finds the stored drawings most like the new one square by square, and the labels of those neighbours vote. Watch it get the first guesses wrong, add more examples and watch the votes firm up. Then teach it a trap: every cat drawn in the top corner, every house at the bottom, and see it decide by position instead of shape.
takeaway: A machine learns to sort things by comparing new examples with the ones it was shown, so more and more varied examples make it better, and a lazy pattern in the examples teaches it the wrong thing.
needs: Optional: doodles from the Quick, Draw! dataset (Google, CC BY 4.0) as a ready pile of examples; the reader's own drawings need nothing.
needsSource: Quick, Draw! dataset, CC BY 4.0 (https://github.com/googlecreativelab/quickdraw-dataset), optional.
pitfall: The machine does not know what a cat is; it compares squares. Do not call the neighbour vote a neural network; neural-networks comes later. The trap where every wolf photo had snow is real and belongs on the page.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 3, Learning, in the AAAI/CSTA K-12 AI guidelines (https://ai4k12.org/).
overlapWith: learning-from-data (level 1): that page fits a curve to points and shows overfitting with a test set; this one classifies drawings by nearest neighbours with no curve and no error plot, and leads into it.

title: How a speaker hears its name
interaction: Say 'go' or 'stop' into the microphone (or pick one of the shipped recordings of other people saying it) and step through what the speaker does: the sound becomes a picture, time left to right and pitch bottom to top, with the loud parts bright; a small trained network that has looked at thousands of such pictures lights a confidence bar for each word it knows. Whisper, add kitchen noise or say a word it never learned, and watch the bars fall or the 'unknown' bar rise. The page says which words the network knows and that everything after the wake word goes to a bigger computer.
takeaway: A voice assistant turns sound into a picture of pitches over time, and a small network that has seen thousands of people say the word recognises the shape, which is why noise and unfamiliar voices trip it.
needs: A small keyword-spotting model that runs in the browser: the TensorFlow.js speech-commands model (Apache 2.0), trained on the Speech Commands dataset (CC BY 4.0), whose vocabulary is the digits plus up, down, left, right, go, stop, yes and no; plus a handful of shipped clips from that dataset for readers who decline the microphone.
needsSource: TensorFlow.js speech-commands model (Apache 2.0, https://github.com/tensorflow/tfjs-models/tree/master/speech-commands) and Speech Commands v2 (CC BY 4.0).
pitfall: The wake-word listener does not understand words and does not send everything it hears: the small network runs on the device and knows only a few words, and the rest is sent only after it fires. It is not matching against one recording of the owner.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 1, Perception (https://ai4k12.org/); 'Virtual assistant' averaged about 7,400 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Virtual_assistant/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: convolution-vision (level 2) inspects a trained image classifier layer by layer on drawn digits; here the input is sound, the picture is the spectrogram the reader watches being made, and the network is a box with confidence bars. language-models is what runs after the wake word.

title: Why the app says 'you might also like'
interaction: Start on any article in a small web of real Wikipedia pages and see where its readers went next, as arrows whose thickness is a count; the 'you might also like' box is just the thickest arrows. Pick a different starting page and the box changes; follow a few arrows yourself and watch the suggestions drift toward the most-visited pages, which turn up in nearly everyone's box. Then add a brand-new page with no visits and see that nothing can recommend it yet.
takeaway: 'You might also like' is a count of where other people went after the same thing you are looking at, so it pulls everyone toward the popular and has nothing to say about anything new.
needs: A small subset of the Wikipedia Clickstream (monthly referer-to-article counts, CC0), e.g. the neighbourhood of a few dozen articles.
needsSource: Wikimedia Clickstream, CC0 (https://dumps.wikimedia.org/other/clickstream/). No open user-by-film ratings set was found (MovieLens is research-use only), so 'people like you' from ratings is not built here; the page is item-to-item counts.
pitfall: The app does not know you; it knows counts of other people's paths, or in shops their purchases. Do not present the suggestion as taste or understanding, and show the pull toward the popular and the empty box for a new item rather than hiding them.
why: AI4K12 Big Idea 3, Learning (https://ai4k12.org/); 'Recommender system' averaged about 7,700 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Recommender_system/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: pagerank (level 2): that page ranks pages by who links to whom with a random surfer; this one uses counts of actual reader paths from one page to the next, and the output is a 'next' list, not a ranking of the whole web. learning-from-data fits a model; here there is only counting.

title: Clustering
interaction: Scatter points by hand or load a real dataset of penguins measured by bill and flipper, then step k-means: drop k centres, colour every point by its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its colour, and repeat until nothing moves. Change k and the starting positions and watch the result change, plot the total distance against k to choose a number of groups, and try a cloud shaped like two rings, where k-means fails and a method that follows density succeeds.
takeaway: A computer can find groups in data with no labels at all, by alternately assigning points to the nearest centre and moving the centres, but which groups it finds depends on how many it is told to look for and where it starts.
needs: A small real dataset with natural clusters.
needsSource: the Palmer penguins dataset (CC0)
pitfall: k-means does not discover the number of groups and finds only compact round blobs; the elbow plot is a heuristic. Different starts give different answers, so run it several times.
why: Google's 'Introduction to Clustering' course (choose a similarity measure, cluster with k-means, evaluate the result) https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/clustering
overlapWith: learning-from-data fits labelled points and embeddings shows a map of words that cluster; neither runs the algorithm that finds groups without labels. The pool's clustering-gaussian-mixtures (level 3) is EM on Gaussian mixtures; this is the level-1 k-means by hand.

title: Momentum, Adam & learning-rate schedules
interaction: Race plain gradient descent, momentum, RMSProp and Adam on a bowl whose condition number you set with a slider: stretch it a thousand to one and watch plain descent zigzag or stall while Adam's per-parameter step sizes, drawn as arrows, rescale the long axis. Tune momentum past critical damping to see it oscillate, then add warmup and a cosine schedule and compare how each optimizer finishes on a small real network's loss curve.
takeaway: Gradient descent is slow when the loss is stretched more along some parameters than others, and momentum, per-parameter scaling and schedules each fix a different part of that.
pitfall: Adam does not find better minima, it reaches them faster, and on some problems plain momentum generalizes better; do not declare a winner. The momentum analysis is exact only for quadratics, say so.
why: Distill, Why Momentum Really Works (Goh 2017): https://distill.pub/2017/momentum/
overlapWith: gradient-descent: that page already offers a momentum toggle on ravines and plateaus; here the ravine's conditioning is the control, and per-parameter scaling (RMSProp, Adam) and schedules are new.
needsSource: none

title: Adversarial examples
interaction: Draw a digit for a small classifier running in the browser, then drag an epsilon slider: the page adds epsilon times the sign of the loss gradient, an image you can see beside the digit, and the prediction flips from 3 to 8 while the drawn digit looks unchanged. Compare a random perturbation of the same size, which does nothing, then switch to a model trained adversarially and see the flip need a visible epsilon and the clean accuracy fall.
takeaway: Because a classifier is nearly linear in its input, a tiny step along the gradient of its loss, invisible to the eye, flips its output, while random noise of the same size does not.
needs: A small digit classifier with backpropagation to the input in the browser, trained on MNIST (CC BY-SA 3.0) as the existing convolution-vision page's drawn-digit classifier is, plus an adversarially trained twin; the page ships only its own weights, no images.
pitfall: Adversarial examples are not a bug of one model; they transfer between models trained separately. The perturbation is not noise, and robustness is bought with clean accuracy.
why: Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy 2015, Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples: https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6572
overlapWith: convolution-vision: that page inspects what a classifier responds to; this one attacks the same kind of classifier through its gradient.
needsSource: MNIST, CC BY-SA 3.0 (confirmed); only own trained weights are shipped, following the data decision of convolution-vision.

title: Clustering: k-means & Gaussian mixtures
interaction: Scatter points or load the Palmer penguins without their labels and step k-means: assign each point to its nearest centre, move the centres, repeat; try several k and seeds and watch it fail on elongated clusters. Switch to expectation-maximization on a Gaussian mixture, where each point is colored by its soft responsibilities, the ellipses stretch to fit and the log-likelihood climbs; then watch a density-based method pick out a ring that both of the others cut in half.
takeaway: Clustering is fitting a model of groups without labels, and each algorithm's idea of a group, nearest centre, Gaussian blob or dense region, decides what it can and cannot find.
needs: Palmer penguins dataset (CC0).
pitfall: k-means returns k clusters whether or not they exist, so show it carving a single blob; EM finds a local maximum that depends on the start.
why: Stanford CS229 fall 2021 syllabus, k-means, expectation-maximization and mixtures of Gaussians: https://cs229.stanford.edu/syllabus-fall2021.html
overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page fits labeled points; here there are no labels and the algorithm's assumption about group shape is what is on display.
needsSource: Palmer penguins, CC0 (from memory, unverified in this session).

title: Contrastive & self-supervised learning
interaction: Train a small encoder on unlabeled clothing images where the only signal is agreement: two random augmentations (crop, flip, blur) of the same image are pulled together on a unit circle of embeddings and all other images are pushed apart. Watch the circle sort itself into clothing types without ever seeing a label, slide the temperature to make the negatives push harder or softer, then flip to the CLIP variant where a grid of image-text similarities is trained to light up only on its diagonal.
takeaway: A representation can be learned with no labels by making a network agree with itself across augmentations and disagree with other examples, and the augmentations decide what the representation learns to ignore.
needs: A Fashion-MNIST subset (MIT); the encoder trains live or is scrubbed from precomputed checkpoints (own weights).
pitfall: Self-supervised is not unsupervised clustering: the augmentations are a design choice that injects knowledge. Collapse, every embedding equal, is the failure to show.
why: Chen et al. 2020, SimCLR, A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations: https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05709
overlapWith: embeddings: that page explores a given embedding space; this one shows how such a space is trained without labels.
needsSource: Fashion-MNIST, MIT licence (confirmed); own weights.

title: Dimensionality reduction: PCA & t-SNE
interaction: Rotate a 3-D cloud of points and watch its shadow on the screen: the principal axes are the rotation that keeps the most spread, and dropping the third axis loses the least. Then run t-SNE live on a few hundred clothing images: the map forms as the gradient steps run, and sliding the perplexity or reseeding rearranges it, which shows what is real (who neighbours whom) and what is an artefact (cluster sizes and the gaps between them).
takeaway: PCA keeps the directions of largest variance and nothing else, while t-SNE keeps each point's neighbours and sacrifices everything else, so the two maps answer different questions.
needs: A Fashion-MNIST subset (MIT).
pitfall: Distances between t-SNE clusters and their sizes mean nothing; the page must not read them. Principal components are directions of variance, not the features that matter for a task.
why: Distill, How to Use t-SNE Effectively: https://distill.pub/2016/misread-tsne/
overlapWith: embeddings: that page's pitfall warns that its 2-D map distorts distances; this page is about how such maps are made and exactly what each one distorts.
needsSource: Fashion-MNIST, MIT licence (confirmed).

title: Bias, variance & double descent
interaction: Fit random-feature ridge regression to noisy data and slide the number of features from a few to many times the number of points: the test error rises, peaks exactly where the model can first fit every point, then falls again, while the training error hits zero and stays there. Resample the training set many times to see the fits' spread (variance) and their average's miss (bias), add label noise to sharpen the peak, and add ridge regularization to erase it.
takeaway: Test error peaks where a model has just enough parameters to memorize its data and falls again beyond it, so models larger than their data can generalize, and regularization smooths the peak away.
pitfall: The classical U-shaped curve is not wrong, it is the left half. The second descent needs the minimum-norm (or implicitly regularized) solution; with an arbitrary interpolating fit it does not happen.
why: OpenAI, Deep Double Descent (Nakkiran et al. 2019): https://openai.com/index/deep-double-descent
overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page stops where the test error turns upward; this one keeps adding parameters through the interpolation peak and down the other side.
needsSource: none

title: Dropout, weight decay & batch normalization
interaction: Build a small network on a 2-D dataset from a palette that includes dropout and batch-norm layers and train it live: the decision boundary, the weight histogram and each layer's activation distribution update as it learns. Switch dropout on to see many thinned sub-networks' boundaries and their average; add weight decay and watch the weights shrink and the boundary smooth; add batch norm, raise the learning rate tenfold and see the activations stay centred where the plain network's blow up.
takeaway: Dropout trains an ensemble of thinned networks at once, weight decay keeps the function smooth, and batch norm keeps each layer's inputs in range so training survives large steps.
pitfall: Dropout is off at test time with activations rescaled, and batch norm behaves differently in training and inference; the page must show both modes. Do not state that batch norm works by removing internal covariate shift as established fact.
why: Stanford CS231n, lecture Training Neural Networks (dropout, batch normalization, weight decay): https://cs231n.stanford.edu/schedule.html
overlapWith: neural-networks: that page builds and trains plain layers; this one adds the regularizers and the normalization and shows what each does to the weights and activations.
needsSource: none

title: Evolutionary algorithms
interaction: Release a population on the landscapes gradient descent uses, plus a jagged one with no useful gradient: CMA-ES draws its population as an ellipse that stretches along the valley and shrinks as it converges, with mutation strength and population size as sliders. Then run a genetic algorithm on a discrete problem, a short tour through cities, with crossover, mutation and selection pressure as controls, and watch diversity collapse when selection is too strong.
takeaway: A population under selection, mutation and recombination can climb a landscape with no gradient at all, and the spread of the population is the search's memory of which directions worked.
pitfall: Evolutionary search is an optimizer, not a model of biology; fitness is a function the designer chose. Do not present the genetic algorithm as the method of choice: CMA-ES is what is used on continuous problems.
why: David Ha, A Visual Guide to Evolution Strategies: https://blog.otoro.net/2017/10/29/visual-evolution-strategies/
overlapWith: evolution: that page shows natural selection acting on creatures at level 1; here selection, mutation and recombination are optimizers on a fitness landscape, compared with gradient descent.
needsSource: none

title: Federated learning & differential privacy
interaction: Split a 2-D dataset across several devices, each holding its own skewed slice, and run federated averaging: every device trains locally for a few steps, sends its update, and the server averages them into one model whose boundary is drawn on every device. Make the slices more unlike each other and watch client drift pull the average off course; then clip each update and add noise with a privacy budget slider and see the accuracy paid for every notch of privacy.
takeaway: A model can be trained without the data leaving the devices by averaging their updates, and the privacy of each update is bought with clipping and noise that cost accuracy.
pitfall: Federated learning alone is not private: gradients can leak training data, which is why differential privacy is added. Epsilon is a bound on how much one person's data can change the output, not a probability of a leak.
why: McMahan et al. 2017, Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data: https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.05629
overlapWith: neural-networks: that page trains on one dataset in one place; here the data is split over devices, averaging is the mechanism and privacy noise is the trade.
needsSource: none

title: Gaussian processes
interaction: Click to add observations on a blank axis and watch the posterior mean and its 95% band snap to them with sample functions drawn through; the band pinches to nothing at the data and swells between points. Drag the kernel's length scale and noise, swap kernels (squared exponential, periodic, linear) with the kernel matrix shown as a heat map alongside, then let the page choose the next point to query by upper confidence bound, the step at the heart of Bayesian optimization.
takeaway: A Gaussian process is a distribution over functions set by a kernel, and conditioning it on data pins it down where observed and leaves uncertainty that grows with distance from the data at a rate the kernel sets.
pitfall: Draw sample functions, not only the mean and band; the mean alone looks like any smoother. The band's width away from data comes from the prior, not from evidence.
why: Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, the standard text, free online: https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/
overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page fits one curve; here the fit is a whole distribution of curves and the uncertainty between data points is the point.
needsSource: none

title: Generative adversarial networks
interaction: Choose a 2-D dataset (a ring of eight Gaussians, a spiral) and train a tiny generator and discriminator live: the generator's cloud of samples chases the data while the discriminator's verdict is painted underneath as a field. Unbalance the two learning rates or shrink the discriminator and watch mode collapse, the cloud settling on one blob and hopping between them; then scrub precomputed sample grids from a GAN trained on clothing images epoch by epoch.
takeaway: Two networks play a game, one forging samples and one judging them, and the forger learns the data distribution only through the judge's verdicts, which is why training oscillates and can collapse onto a few modes.
needs: None for the live 2-D case; precomputed sample grids from a small GAN trained offline on Fashion-MNIST (MIT), own weights.
pitfall: GAN losses are not a progress meter: a falling generator loss says nothing about sample quality, so the page must not draw the loss as a curve to be minimized. Do not claim a GAN memorizes training images.
why: MIT 6.S191 2025 lecture 4, Deep Generative Modeling, and Stanford CS236: https://introtodeeplearning.com/2025/index.html
overlapWith: diffusion-models: its 2-D cloud is denoised through many fixed steps; here one network maps noise to data in a single pass and the only learning signal is a second network's judgement.
needsSource: Fashion-MNIST, MIT licence (confirmed) for the precomputed image samples; own weights.

title: Graph neural networks
interaction: On Zachary's karate club (34 members, two factions) label two members and step message passing one layer at a time: each node's vector becomes an aggregate of its neighbours', drawn as a 2-D embedding that moves at every layer, and the faction prediction spreads outward from the two seeds. Keep stacking layers and watch every embedding converge to one point, then show two different graphs that every such network embeds identically.
takeaway: A graph network updates each node from its neighbours' messages, so after k layers a node summarizes its k-hop neighbourhood, and with too many layers every node summarizes the same thing.
needs: Zachary's karate-club graph (34 nodes, Table 3 of Zachary 1977, redistributed with NetworkX).
pitfall: Message passing is not PageRank: the aggregation weights are learned. The Weisfeiler-Lehman limit means some non-isomorphic graphs are indistinguishable to message passing, and the page should show a pair.
why: Stanford CS224W 2023 slides on message passing and GNN expressive power: https://snap.stanford.edu/class/cs224w-2023/slides/07-theory.pdf
overlapWith: pagerank: that page propagates a scalar along links by a fixed rule; here vectors propagate with learned weights, and oversmoothing and the expressiveness limit are new.
needsSource: Zachary karate club: 34-node table from a 1977 paper, widely redistributed, licence unverified; trivially small and could be re-entered from the paper with citation.

title: Induction heads & in-context learning
interaction: Scrub through the training run of a tiny two-layer attention-only transformer trained on repeated random token sequences (checkpoints precomputed): the loss on the second copy of each sequence drops suddenly at one point of training, and hovering any token shows the attention pattern at that checkpoint. Before the drop the heads attend diffusely; after it, one head in the first layer attends to the previous token and one in the second attends to the token that followed the current token's last occurrence, and ablating either head erases the drop live.
takeaway: In-context copying is done by a two-head circuit, a previous-token head feeding an induction head, and it appears abruptly during training, which is why the loss curve has a step.
needs: The project's own precomputed checkpoints of a tiny attention-only transformer (a vocabulary of tens of tokens, two layers), run in the browser.
pitfall: The circuit is established in small attention-only models; in large models the evidence is correlational, say so. Attention weights are not explanations on their own; the ablation is the evidence.
why: Anthropic, In-context Learning and Induction Heads (Olsson et al. 2022): https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html
overlapWith: transformers: that page shows a trained model's attention on sentences; this one shows a circuit of two heads forming during training and tests it by ablation.
needsSource: none external; own checkpoints

title: Speech recognition: from sound to letters
interaction: Pick a one-second spoken word from the Speech Commands set, or say one into the microphone, and step it through the pipeline: waveform, spectrogram, mel features, then a small network's per-frame letter probabilities drawn as a lattice. Watch connectionist temporal classification collapse the frames, repeats and blanks, into the word, and drag the alignment to see why the model never needs to know where each letter starts.
takeaway: Speech recognition turns a spectrogram into a letter probability per time slice and then collapses repeats and blanks, so the network is never told where each sound begins and ends.
needs: A subset of Google's Speech Commands v2 (CC BY 4.0, with a no-speaker-identification condition) and a small CTC model trained on it offline (own weights).
pitfall: This is isolated-word recognition; continuous speech adds a language model and beam-search decoding, say so. Do not say the network hears phonemes.
why: Speech Commands dataset card, CC BY 4.0: https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/speech_commands ; Stanford CS224S Spoken Language Processing covers CTC.
overlapWith: fourier-transform: that page turns a signal into frequencies; this one continues from the spectrogram to letters and shows the CTC alignment.
needsSource: Google Speech Commands v2, CC BY 4.0 (confirmed); own trained weights.

title: Mixture of experts
interaction: Assemble a layer from a palette of small expert networks and a router, set how many experts each input may use, and train it on a 2-D regression: the plane is tiled by which expert each input is routed to, each expert's own fit is drawn in its tile, and a histogram counts inputs per expert. Remove the load-balancing loss and watch one expert take every input while the others idle; a counter shows parameters stored against parameters used per input.
takeaway: A router sends each input to a few of many experts, so a model can hold far more parameters than it spends per token, and routing collapses onto one expert unless a balancing term pushes traffic apart.
pitfall: Experts do not specialize by topic as the name suggests; in real language models they split by token-level patterns. The top-k choice is discrete, so show that the gate's softmax weight is what carries the gradient.
why: Hugging Face, Mixture of Experts Explained: https://huggingface.co/blog/moe
overlapWith: transformers: that page shows attention mixing tokens; this one replaces the feed-forward block with routed experts and shows the compute-per-token against total-parameters trade.
needsSource: none

title: Monte Carlo tree search & AlphaGo
interaction: Play Connect Four against the page and step its thinking one simulation at a time: selection walks down the tree by the upper-confidence rule, expansion adds a node, a random rollout plays the game to the end, and the result is backed up as visit counts and win rates, so the tree grows lopsided toward promising moves. Set the simulation budget and the exploration constant, then replace the random rollouts with a small value and policy network trained by self-play and see the same budget play far better.
takeaway: Tree search can play well with no rules of thumb by sampling games and growing the tree where the samples look best, and a learned value network in place of random rollouts is the AlphaGo idea.
needs: None for the search itself; a small Connect Four policy and value network trained by self-play offline (own weights).
pitfall: MCTS is not minimax with random tie-breaking; the asymmetric growth is the point. AlphaGo's networks did not replace search, they guided it.
why: Silver et al. 2016, Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search, Nature: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16961
overlapWith: graph-search: that page finds shortest paths in a known graph; here the tree is grown by sampling under uncertainty and value estimates decide where it grows.
needsSource: none external; own weights

title: Normalizing flows
interaction: Stack invertible layers (an affine coupling layer, a rotation, an elementwise squash) and drag their parameters: a grid drawn on the plane warps, and the Gaussian base density is recolored by the exact change-of-variables rule, dense where the map squeezes space and thin where it stretches it. Then train the stack on two-moons data and watch the Gaussian flow into the data; run it backwards to see samples born from noise.
takeaway: A chain of invertible maps with a cheap Jacobian is a generative model whose likelihood is exact: the density at a point is the base density at its preimage times how much the map shrank space there.
pitfall: The log-determinant must come from the layer structure (coupling layers make the Jacobian triangular); estimating the density from sample histograms is exactly what flows avoid. Say that flow matching is a different, later idea.
why: Stanford CS236 Deep Generative Models covers flow models alongside VAEs and GANs: https://bulletin.stanford.edu/courses/2205691
overlapWith: linear-transformations: that page warps a grid with one 2x2 matrix; here nonlinear invertible layers warp a probability density and the determinant becomes a likelihood.
needsSource: none

title: Recommender systems & collaborative filtering
interaction: Rate a dozen films and watch a matrix-factorization model, two hidden factors per person and per film fit by alternating least squares live, place you and the films on a 2-D map and fill in your blank ratings. Add factors and regularization and see the held-out error curve; add a new film with no ratings and see cold start, and watch popularity bias as the most-rated films are recommended to everyone.
takeaway: Recommendations come from factoring the sparse ratings table into a few hidden tastes per person and per item, so people who rated like you did are your prediction, and an item nobody has rated cannot be placed.
needs: A ratings dataset. MovieLens ml-latest-small (GroupLens) permits redistribution only under its research, non-commercial conditions, which is not an open licence; this candidate's data is weak unless an openly licensed ratings set is found.
pitfall: The factors are not genres; do not name them. Held-out ratings are a biased test because people choose what to rate.
why: Stanford CS246 Mining Massive Data Sets, recommender systems lectures: http://web.stanford.edu/class/cs246/ ; MovieLens terms: https://files.grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/ml-latest-small-README.html
overlapWith: embeddings: that page maps words from pretrained vectors; here the vectors are learned live from a ratings table and the problem is the missing entries.
needsSource: MovieLens ml-latest-small: research-only, non-commercial redistribution terms (confirmed), not an open licence; weak.

title: Recurrent networks & LSTMs
interaction: Feed a sequence symbol by symbol into a plain recurrent network and an LSTM trained to recall its first symbol after a gap you set: the hidden state and the LSTM's forget, input and output gates are drawn at each step. Then run backpropagation through time and watch the gradient reaching the early steps shrink geometrically in the plain network while the LSTM's cell state carries it almost unchanged; lengthen the gap until the plain network fails and the LSTM still works.
takeaway: A recurrent network carries a state from step to step, and gates that choose what to keep let a signal, and its gradient, travel far back through time without vanishing.
pitfall: Vanishing gradients come from repeated multiplication by the same Jacobian, not from forgetting; show the gradient norms, not a metaphor. LSTMs mitigate the problem, they do not remove it, and saturated gates stop learning.
why: MIT 6.S191 2025, lecture 2 Deep Sequence Modeling (RNNs, LSTMs): https://introtodeeplearning.com/2025/index.html
overlapWith: transformers: that page mixes all tokens at once with attention; here the model is sequential with a carried state and the question is how far a signal survives.
needsSource: none

title: Retrieval-augmented generation
interaction: Assemble a retrieval pipeline over a few thousand Simple English Wikipedia paragraphs: choose the chunk size, keyword (BM25) or embedding search and how many chunks to keep, then type a question and watch the chunks ranked live with their scores and the prompt assembled from them. For a fixed set of questions, flip between the model's precomputed answer with and without the retrieved chunks and see the answer follow the chunks: right when the fact was retrieved, fluently wrong when it was not.
takeaway: A language model can only use what is in its prompt, so retrieval decides what it can quote, and the chunking and ranking, not the model, is where most answers are won or lost.
needs: A Simple English Wikipedia extract (CC BY-SA 4.0); embeddings computed in the browser or precomputed with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0); precomputed answers from a small openly licensed model (an Apache-2.0 Qwen or SmolLM checkpoint).
pitfall: Retrieval does not make a model truthful; it will quote a wrong chunk fluently. Keyword and dense search fail on different questions, so show both.
why: Lewis et al. 2020, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
overlapWith: embeddings: that page finds the nearest words in vector space; this one feeds the nearest passages to a generator and shows the generation change.
needsSource: Simple English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0; all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Apache 2.0 (from memory, unverified); answer model licence to confirm when chosen.

title: RLHF: learning from human preferences
interaction: Read pairs of continuations that a real small language model wrote for a prompt and click the better one; a reward model (a linear layer on each continuation's sentence embedding, fit by the Bradley-Terry rule) updates after every click and scores all the candidates. Slide the KL penalty: the policy, computed exactly as the base model's distribution tilted by exp(reward/beta), drifts from the base model toward the reward model's favourites, and with a small penalty it collapses onto whichever odd continuation the reward model over-rates, reward hacking visible in the ranked list.
takeaway: Comparisons train a reward model, and the policy is the base model's distribution pulled toward that reward and held back by a KL leash; loosen the leash and the policy exploits the reward model's mistakes instead of the preferences behind them.
needs: For a handful of prompts, about 64 sampled continuations each with reference log-probabilities from GPT-2 small (OpenAI, modified MIT licence) and one sentence embedding per continuation from an open embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Apache 2.0), all precomputed.
pitfall: RLHF teaches no new facts; it reweights outputs the base model could already produce. On a finite candidate set the KL-regularized optimum is closed-form, so the page must not pretend PPO is running; say that DPO uses the same closed form.
why: Hugging Face, Illustrating RLHF (reward model, KL penalty): https://huggingface.co/blog/rlhf ; Stanford CS224N has an RLHF lecture (slide archive https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs224n/cs224n.1246/slides/).
overlapWith: reinforcement-learning: that page learns values from rewards painted on a grid; here the reward itself is learned from comparisons and the environment is a language model's own output distribution.
needsSource: GPT-2 weights, OpenAI modified MIT (confirmed); all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Apache 2.0 (from memory, unverified); the continuations and labels are generated by the project.

title: Scaling laws
interaction: Scrub a precomputed sweep of small networks trained with growing width and data on one task and watch the loss fall as a straight line on log-log axes until the data or the model runs out, then retrain one point of the sweep live and see it land on the line. Switch to the Chinchilla parametric law and drag a compute budget: the page solves for the model size and token count that minimize the fitted loss, drawing the iso-compute curves and the optimal frontier.
takeaway: Loss falls as a power law in model size and in data, each saturating when the other is the bottleneck, so a given compute budget has an optimal split between the two.
needs: The project's own precomputed sweep of small models; the Chinchilla fit L = E + A/N^a + B/D^b with the constants published by Hoffmann et al. 2022; optionally Epoch AI's re-extracted data points.
pitfall: Scaling laws are empirical fits with disputed constants (Epoch AI's replication); do not present them as physics. The live retrain must be tiny and labelled as such, not a per-slider sweep.
why: Hoffmann et al. 2022, Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556 ; Epoch AI replication: https://epoch.ai/publications/chinchilla-scaling-a-replication-attempt
overlapWith: language-models: that page shows what a trained model does; this one shows how its loss depends on size and data and why models are the sizes they are.
needsSource: Own sweep (none external); Chinchilla constants are published numbers (arXiv paper, licence not checked); Epoch AI extracted data, licence unverified.

title: Superposition & sparse autoencoders
interaction: Train Anthropic's toy model live: more features than hidden neurons, each feature active with a sparsity you set; the learned feature directions are drawn in the hidden plane and go from only the most important features, at right angles, to all of them packed as antipodal pairs and pentagons as the features grow sparser. Then train a sparse autoencoder on the hidden activations and watch its dictionary recover the packed directions one by one.
takeaway: A network can store more features than it has neurons by overlapping them when features are rarely active together, and a sparse autoencoder can pull the overlapped features apart again.
pitfall: Neurons are not features, so do not label individual hidden units. Sparse-autoencoder features are a hypothesis about the model, not ground truth, and the toy model's results do not transfer wholesale to real networks.
why: Anthropic, Toy Models of Superposition: https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html ; DeepMind's Gemma Scope release of open SAEs: https://deepmind.google/blog/gemma-scope-helping-the-safety-community-shed-light-on-the-inner-workings-of-language-models/
overlapWith: embeddings: that page shows meaning as directions in a vector space; here the question is how many directions fit in one layer and how to recover them from a trained network.
needsSource: none (the toy model and the sparse autoencoder train in the browser)

title: Support vector machines & kernels
interaction: Drag labeled points on the plane: a perceptron finds some separating line, then the SVM finds the one with the widest margin, with the support vectors highlighted and every other point free to move without changing it. Lower the penalty C to let points inside the margin, then switch on a polynomial or Gaussian kernel and drag its width to see the straight margin in feature space land as a curved boundary on the plane.
takeaway: The best separating line is the one farthest from the nearest points, which alone determine it, and a kernel lets the same margin-maximizer draw curves by measuring similarity instead of coordinates.
pitfall: The kernel trick never computes the high-dimensional features; the solution depends on the data only through inner products. Kernel width and C trade off flexibility against margin, not accuracy against speed.
why: Stanford CS229 fall 2021 syllabus, lectures on support vector machines and kernels: https://cs229.stanford.edu/syllabus-fall2021.html
overlapWith: neural-networks: that page learns a boundary by backpropagation; here the boundary solves a convex margin problem decided by a few points, and the kernel takes the place of hidden layers.
needsSource: none

title: Tokenization & byte-pair encoding
interaction: Type a small corpus and run byte-pair encoding one merge at a time: the most frequent adjacent pair fuses, the vocabulary grows by one and the token count of a sample sentence falls, plotted as a curve. Then type any text and watch GPT-2's real byte-level tokenizer apply its merges in rank order after the regex pre-split: common English words become one token, a rare word breaks into several pieces, numbers split oddly, and the same sentence in another language or script costs far more tokens.
takeaway: Tokens are greedy merges of the most frequent byte pairs in the training text, so a model sees whole words where text is common and fragments where it is rare, and never sees letters.
needs: GPT-2's merge list and vocabulary (OpenAI; shipped by tiktoken under MIT, the GPT-2 release under a modified MIT licence).
pitfall: Merges apply in rank order, not by longest match, so the split is deterministic given the merge list; byte-level BPE never needs an unknown token. Do not say that models count letters.
why: Hugging Face NLP course, chapter 6, byte-pair encoding tokenization: https://huggingface.co/learn/nlp-course/chapter6/5
overlapWith: language-models: that page splits typed text into tokens as given; this one builds the tokenizer merge by merge and shows why the split falls where it does.
needsSource: tiktoken, MIT (confirmed); the GPT-2 merge and vocabulary files sit in OpenAI's gpt-2 repository under its modified MIT licence (repository licence; the files were not separately checked).

title: Decision trees, random forests & gradient boosting
interaction: Grow a decision tree one split at a time on 2-D points or on the Palmer penguins: each candidate split's impurity drop is shown, the chosen one slices the plane, and the tree deepens until it has memorized every point. Then bag many trees trained on bootstrap resamples and watch the jagged boundary average smooth, and finally boost: each new shallow tree fits the current residuals and the sum of trees staircases toward the data, with the learning rate and depth as sliders and the test error plotted.
takeaway: A single tree slices the plane greedily and overfits, averaging many resampled trees cancels their noise, and boosting adds small trees that each fix what the ensemble still gets wrong.
needs: Palmer penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman; CC0).
pitfall: A random forest does not overfit by adding trees; boosting does. Impurity-based feature importance is biased toward high-cardinality features and is not causal.
why: Stanford CS229 summer 2020 syllabus covers decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting as tree ensembles: https://cs229.stanford.edu/summer2020/syllabus.html
overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page fits one polynomial of growing degree; here axis-aligned splits grow a tree and the ensemble steps, bagging and boosting, are the content.
needsSource: Palmer penguins, CC0 (from memory, unverified in this session).

title: Confidence & calibration
interaction: Train a small classifier on 2-D data and paint its confidence over the plane: it is near certain far from any data, where it has no business being sure. A reliability diagram bins predictions by confidence against how often they are right; drag a temperature slider to rescale the logits and watch the diagram straighten and the calibration error fall, then switch on an ensemble of five networks and see the far-away confidence finally drop where the members disagree.
takeaway: A network's softmax confidence is not its probability of being right; one temperature can fix the calibration on data like the training data, but only disagreement between models reveals where there is no data at all.
pitfall: Temperature scaling changes no predicted class and no accuracy: calibration and accuracy are different things, and a calibrated model can still be confidently wrong off-distribution.
why: Guo et al. 2017, On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks: https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599
overlapWith: gaussian-processes: that page's uncertainty comes from a prior over functions; here it is a trained classifier's confidence and how to correct it.
needsSource: none

title: Autoencoders & variational autoencoders
interaction: Push clothing images through a bottleneck of two numbers and drag the decoded point around the 2-D latent plane: a plain autoencoder's map has holes and jumps, a VAE's is smooth and dense. Click an image to see its encoding drawn as an ellipse rather than a point, then slide the weight of the KL term from zero upward and watch the encodings crowd toward the unit circle while reconstructions blur.
takeaway: A VAE makes each code a distribution pulled toward a standard Gaussian, trading a little reconstruction sharpness for a latent space in which every point decodes to something plausible, so sampling works.
needs: A Fashion-MNIST subset (Zalando, MIT licence) and an autoencoder and a VAE with a 2-D latent trained on it offline (own weights, a few hundred KB) whose decoders run in the browser.
pitfall: A VAE is not an autoencoder with noise added: the KL term regularizes the encoder's distribution, not the decoded image, and the reparameterization trick exists so that gradients pass through the sampling step. The blur comes from the pixel-wise likelihood, not from the latent being small.
why: Stanford CS236 Deep Generative Models lists VAEs, GANs and flow models as its core: https://bulletin.stanford.edu/courses/2205691
overlapWith: diffusion-models: that page generates by denoising noise through many fixed steps; this one compresses through a bottleneck and shows a navigable latent map and the KL trade-off that makes it navigable.
needsSource: Fashion-MNIST, MIT licence (confirmed); trained weights are the project's own.

title: World models & model-based RL
interaction: Let an agent act in a small physical world (a cart balancing a pole) while a small network learns to predict the next state from the current state and action; imagined rollouts are drawn as ghosts over the real ones and drift apart as the horizon grows. Slide the number of planning steps taken in imagination per real step and watch the learning curve steepen, then lengthen the imagined horizon until compounding model error has the agent planning for a world that does not exist.
takeaway: Learning a model of the world lets an agent practice in imagination, which buys sample efficiency as long as imagined rollouts stay shorter than the horizon at which the model's errors compound.
pitfall: A world model is not the true physics; show its error growing with horizon. Model-based learning is not always more sample-efficient, and a wrong model can make the agent worse than model-free learning.
why: Berkeley CS285 fall 2023, lectures 10 to 12 on planning and model-based RL: https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse-fa23/ ; Ha and Schmidhuber 2018, World Models: https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.10122
overlapWith: reinforcement-learning: that page learns values by trial in a grid world; here the agent learns the world's dynamics and plans inside the learned model.
needsSource: none
